title: Maja Chwalinska wins her first WTA title with a comeback in Wuhan
subtitle: The Polish player recovered to beat Sonay Kartal in three sets, adding a WTA 1000 trophy to a season that already included a French Open final. For both finalists, Wuhan marked a significant step forward.
author: ATHENA
body:
Maja Chwalinska won her first WTA Tour title on 18 October, recovering from a losing start to defeat Britain’s Sonay Kartal 2–6, 6–4, 6–2 in the Wuhan Open final.

The victory gave the 25-year-old Pole a WTA 1000 title and another major result beyond her run to this year’s French Open final. Wuhan is an outdoor hard-court tournament, making the success a further demonstration that her game can deliver away from clay.

It was also a final between players whose ranking positions told only part of their stories. Chwalinska entered the week at No. 22; Kartal, returning after a lengthy injury absence, was No. 170.

## A final that changed direction

Kartal initially imposed herself with her forehand, while Chwalinska struggled to keep her varied shots inside the court. Reuters described the eventual champion using changes of direction and even a defensive right-handed lob to disrupt her opponent.

The turning point required more than an inventive shot. According to the WTA’s match report, Chwalinska trailed by a set and a break before recovering. She completed the victory in two hours and 43 minutes, saving three break points while serving for the championship.

Afterwards, she credited Kartal for preventing her from playing freely at the start. Her own improvement, she said, came through greater aggression and more depth on her shots.

“It means a lot. It tastes very sweet,” Chwalinska said in the post-match press conference reported by the WTA.

The result places her in a small group. The tour says she is only the fourth player since the WTA 1000 format began in 2009 to claim her first tour title at that level, following Naomi Osaka, Bianca Andreescu and Victoria Mboko.

## Two different routes to the same stage

Chwalinska had reached the final by beating compatriot and former junior doubles partner Iga Swiatek 7–5, 6–1. Earlier this year, she won nine consecutive matches through qualifying and the main draw to reach the Roland Garros final, according to the WTA.

Kartal’s route carried a different significance. A back injury had kept her out for six months; Wuhan was only her third event since returning, according to the Lawn Tennis Association.

Her run included victories over Belinda Bencic, Jasmine Paolini and Elina Svitolina before she defeated Jelena Ostapenko in two semifinal tie-breaks. Those results gave substance to a comeback that a low ranking alone could obscure.

Before the final, Kartal told the WTA she was playing with more confidence than before her injury. Losing the championship match does not erase that progress, although it leaves the trophy with Chwalinska.

The WTA’s post-match report projected Chwalinska would rise to a career-high No. 11 and Kartal to No. 50. Those were projections, rather than a newly verified ranking list.

For Chwalinska, Wuhan changes the terms of the season: she is no longer only a Grand Slam finalist awaiting a first tour trophy. For Kartal, it provides a substantial result after time away.

Neither story needs to become a promise that determination always defeats injury or uncertainty. What this final offers is more concrete: two women returning to the highest level of competition by different routes, and a champion who changed a match that was moving away from her.

The Athena Perspective.
